decks.title: Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement — Part 1: From Champaran to the dialogues
goals: Explain how Gandhi became a national leader through the campaigns of 1917 and 1918
Describe the Non-Cooperation Movement, its forms, its supporters and how it ended
Describe the Civil Disobedience Movement, the march to Dandi and the dialogues of 1930 to 1932
Present the dispute over separate electorates by stating each side's argument

slides.heading: Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement
slides.body_md: Part 1: **Champaran** to the **dialogues** of the early 1930s.

visual.alt: Flow chart, Part 1 at a glance: Gandhi comes home, then Local campaigns, 1917 to 1918, then Non-Cooperation, 1920 to 1922, then Civil Disobedience and the dialogues
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this chapter we follow Mahatma Gandhi and the nationalist movement. In this part we begin with his return to India and the local campaigns that made him known. Then we study Non-Cooperation and the Salt March, and the talks that followed, always asking how historians know what they tell us.

slides.heading: Gandhi comes home
slides.body_md: Returned in **January 1915** after about two decades in **South Africa**.

visual.caption: Gandhi comes home

slides.narration: Gandhi returned to India in January 1915, after about twenty years in South Africa, where he had first used satyagraha, or non violent resistance. On the advice of Gokhale he spent a year travelling across British India. In February 1916, at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University, he criticised the Indian elite for neglecting the poor.

slides.heading: Three local campaigns
slides.body_md: **Champaran** (1917), **Kheda** and **Ahmedabad** (1918).

visual.caption: Three local campaigns

slides.narration: In 1917 at Champaran in Bihar he took up the cause of indigo peasants, and secured security of tenure and freedom to grow crops of their choice. In 1918 in Kheda in Gujarat he asked the state to remit revenue after a crop failure. At Ahmedabad in 1918 he stood with textile mill workers who wanted better conditions and higher wages.

slides.narration: This timeline sets the chapter in time. Gandhi returns in 1915. Non cooperation runs from 1920 to 1922. Purna swaraj is declared in 1929, the Salt March comes in 1930, and the Pact with Irwin in 1931. Quit India begins in 1942, the transfer of power comes in 1947, and Gandhi is assassinated in 1948.

slides.heading: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
slides.body_md: The **Rowlatt Act** of 1919; firing at **Jallianwala Bagh**, 13 April 1919.

rows: Allowed detention without trial; Gandhi called a countrywide hartal
Troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar; hundreds killed, with estimates varying

visual.alt: Table, Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh. Rowlatt Act, 1919: Allowed detention without trial; Gandhi called a countrywide hartal; 13 April 1919: Troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar; hundreds killed, with estimates varying
visual.caption: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh

slides.narration: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial. Gandhi called a countrywide hartal against it. On 13 April 1919, at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, troops under General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd and killed hundreds. Historians give different estimates of the number, and we should say so rather than quote a single figure.

slides.heading: Non-Cooperation and Khilafat
slides.body_md: A movement of **1920 to 1922**, joined with the **Khilafat** cause.

rows: The Khilafat movement, to restore the Caliphate after the defeat of Ottoman Turkey; it brought Hindus and Muslims together
Boycott of schools, colleges, law courts, government jobs and foreign cloth; surrender of titles
Khadi and the charkha; Hindu-Muslim unity; ending untouchability

visual.alt: Table, The Non-Cooperation Movement. Years: 1920 to 1922; Joined with: The Khilafat movement, to restore the Caliphate after the defeat of Ottoman Turkey; it brought Hindus and Muslims together; Forms: Boycott of schools, colleges, law courts, government jobs and foreign cloth; surrender of titles; Constructive work: Khadi and the charkha; Hindu-Muslim unity; ending untouchability
visual.caption: The Non-Cooperation Movement

slides.narration: The Non Cooperation Movement ran from 1920 to 1922. It was combined with the Khilafat movement, which wanted the Caliphate restored after the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, to bring Hindus and Muslims together. People boycotted schools, colleges, courts, government jobs and foreign cloth, and gave up titles. Constructive work meant khadi, the charkha, unity and ending untouchability.

slides.heading: Who joined, and why
slides.body_md: Groups read the movement **in their own ways**.

rows: Villagers of Gorakhpur, studied by the historian Shahid Amin
Businessmen such as G. D. Birla backed the Congress

visual.alt: Table, How groups understood the movement. Non-payment of taxes: Peasants; Forest laws defied: Tribal groups; Rumours of miraculous powers: Villagers of Gorakhpur, studied by the historian Shahid Amin; Support from business: Businessmen such as G. D. Birla backed the Congress
visual.caption: How groups understood the movement

slides.narration: Different groups understood the movement in their own ways. Peasants withheld taxes. Tribal groups defied forest laws. Rumours of miraculous powers spread among villagers, as the historian Shahid Amin found in Gorakhpur. Gandhi dressed simply and spoke the language of ordinary people, and businessmen such as G D Birla supported the Congress.

slides.heading: Chauri Chaura and the end
slides.body_md: **February 1922**: violence, then the movement is **called off**.

nodes.label: Six years for sedition; released in 1924 on health grounds

visual.alt: Flow chart, The end of Non-Cooperation: Chauri Chaura, February 1922, then Gandhi calls off the movement, then Arrest, March 1922, then Six years for sedition; released in 1924 on health grounds
visual.caption: The end of Non-Cooperation

slides.narration: In February 1922, at Chauri Chaura, a crowd set fire to a police station and policemen were killed. Gandhi called off the movement, because it was meant to be non violent. He was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years for sedition, and was released in 1924 on grounds of health. Some leaders and followers were disappointed.

Names a Khilafat committee as a partner

visual.alt: Table, Dating an undated leaflet. Urges a boycott of law courts and foreign cloth: The programme of 1920 to 1922; Names a Khilafat committee as a partner: The alliance still in force; Says nothing about salt or Dandi: Before 1930; Conclusion: About 1920 to 1922
visual.caption: Dating an undated leaflet

slides.narration: Take an imagined undated leaflet. It urges a boycott of courts and foreign cloth, which was the programme of Non Cooperation. It names a Khilafat committee as a partner, so that alliance was still alive. It says nothing of salt, so it comes before 1930. We date it to about 1920 to 1922, as a range.

slides.heading: Simon, Lahore and Independence Day
slides.body_md: Boycott of the **Simon Commission**; **purna swaraj** at Lahore in **1929**.

rows: The all-British Simon Commission is boycotted
Lahore session under Jawaharlal Nehru declares purna swaraj, complete independence

visual.alt: Table, From the Simon Commission to Lahore. 1928: The all-British Simon Commission is boycotted; December 1929: Lahore session under Jawaharlal Nehru declares purna swaraj, complete independence; 26 January 1930: Celebrated as Independence Day
visual.caption: From the Simon Commission to Lahore

slides.narration: In 1928 the all British Simon Commission was boycotted. In December 1929 the Congress met at Lahore, with Jawaharlal Nehru as president, and declared purna swaraj, complete independence, as its goal. The twenty sixth of January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day. The stage was set for a new movement.

slides.heading: Salt and the march to Dandi
slides.body_md: Against the state's **monopoly on salt**: **12 March** to **6 April 1930**.

nodes.label: Letter to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin
12 March 1930: sets out from the Sabarmati ashram

visual.alt: Flow chart, The march to Dandi: Letter to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, then 12 March 1930: sets out from the Sabarmati ashram, then About 240 miles on foot, then 6 April 1930: makes salt at Dandi
visual.caption: The march to Dandi

slides.narration: Gandhi chose the salt law, the state monopoly on making and selling salt. He wrote to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, in advance. On 12 March 1930 he set out from the Sabarmati ashram. After about two hundred and forty miles on foot he reached Dandi on the coast on 6 April and made salt. Foreign newspapers reported the march.

slides.heading: How civil disobedience spread
slides.body_md: Salt, forest laws, taxes, cloth, and **women** in large numbers.

rows: Made in defiance of the state monopoly in many places
Gandhi arrested in May 1930; foreign newspapers carried reports

visual.alt: Table, How civil disobedience spread. Salt: Made in defiance of the state monopoly in many places; Forest laws: Broken; Taxes: Withheld in some areas; Foreign cloth: Boycotted; Women: Took part widely; The state: Gandhi arrested in May 1930; foreign newspapers carried reports
visual.caption: How civil disobedience spread

slides.narration: Civil disobedience spread across the country. Salt was made in many places. Forest laws were broken, taxes were withheld in some areas, and foreign cloth was boycotted. Women took part widely. The government answered with arrests, and Gandhi himself was arrested in May 1930. The movement had become a countrywide protest.

slides.heading: The dialogues of 1930 to 1931
slides.body_md: Round Table Conferences and the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact**.

rows: First Round Table Conference in London, without the Congress
Gandhi-Irwin Pact: civil disobedience called off, prisoners released, salt manufacture along the coast allowed
Second Round Table Conference; Gandhi the Congress's sole representative; no agreement
Civil disobedience resumed, then wound down

visual.alt: Table, The dialogues of 1930 to 1931. November 1930: First Round Table Conference in London, without the Congress; March 1931: Gandhi-Irwin Pact: civil disobedience called off, prisoners released, salt manufacture along the coast allowed; Late 1931: Second Round Table Conference; Gandhi the Congress's sole representative; no agreement; After: Civil disobedience resumed, then wound down
visual.caption: The dialogues of 1930 to 1931

slides.narration: The First Round Table Conference met in London in November 1930, without the Congress. In March 1931 the Gandhi Irwin Pact called off civil disobedience, released prisoners and allowed salt manufacture along the coast. Gandhi then attended the Second Round Table Conference as the sole Congress representative. It failed, because others challenged the Congress claim to speak for everyone.

slides.heading: Separate electorates: two arguments
slides.body_md: The dispute of **1932**: each side's argument.
columns: **Ambedkar:** the depressed classes needed their own representatives, chosen by their own voters, to have a real political voice.
**Gandhi:** separate electorates would divide Hindu society for good; he fasted in opposition.

rows: British announce separate electorates for the depressed classes, the Communal Award
Poona Pact with Ambedkar: reserved seats in the general electorates instead

visual.alt: Table, Separate electorates and the Poona Pact. 1932: British announce separate electorates for the depressed classes, the Communal Award; Gandhi: Fasts in opposition; September 1932: Poona Pact with Ambedkar: reserved seats in the general electorates instead
visual.caption: Separate electorates and the Poona Pact

slides.narration: In 1932 the British announced separate electorates for the depressed classes. Ambedkar argued that they needed their own representatives, chosen by their own voters. Gandhi opposed this, fearing a lasting division of Hindu society, and he fasted. The Poona Pact of September 1932 settled the matter with reserved seats in the general electorates.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: weighing two arguments
slides.body_md: Imagined question: *Who was right in 1932?* A historian's method, step by step.
bullets: Step 1 — State each argument as that side put it.
Step 2 — Name what each side **feared**.
Step 3 — Do not choose a side without **evidence**.
Step 4 — Record the **compromise**.

rows: State each argument as that side put it
Do not choose a side unless the evidence decides it

visual.alt: Table, Weighing two arguments. 1: State each argument as that side put it; 2: Name what each side feared; 3: Do not choose a side unless the evidence decides it; 4: Record the compromise reached
visual.caption: Weighing two arguments

slides.narration: When two leaders disagree, do not begin by taking a side. State each argument as that side put it. Name what each feared: one feared the lack of an own voice, the other a lasting division. Choose a side only if evidence decides the matter. Then record the compromise, here reserved seats in the general electorates.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Table, Summary of Part 1. Emergence: Return in 1915; Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad; Non-Cooperation: 1920 to 1922; Khilafat; boycott; Chauri Chaura; Civil Disobedience: Lahore 1929; Dandi 1930; salt; Dialogues: Pact 1931; failed conference; Poona Pact 1932; Ministries: 8 of 11 provinces in 1937
visual.caption: Summary of Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up. Gandhi returned in 1915 and became known through Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. Non cooperation, joined with Khilafat, ran from 1920 to 1922 and ended after Chauri Chaura. Purna swaraj in 1929, the march to Dandi in 1930, the pact of 1931, the failed conference and the Poona Pact of 1932 followed. The Congress won eight of eleven provinces in 1937.

slides.heading: Quit India and the last days
slides.body_md: Part 2: **Quit India**, the **last days**, and **sources**.

slides.narration: In this part we follow the nationalist movement from the Second World War to Gandhi's death. We study the Quit India movement, then the troubled years of 1946 and 1947, described briefly and without blame. Last, we ask how we can know Gandhi at all: from which sources, and how should we read them.

slides.body_md: The war began in **1939**; the Congress ministries **resigned**.

visual.caption: War, resignations and Lahore 1940

slides.narration: The Second World War began in September 1939. The Viceroy declared India at war without consulting Indians, and the Congress ministries resigned in October and November 1939. In 1940, at Lahore, the Muslim League adopted a resolution demanding independent states for the areas where Muslims were in a majority. The two parties held different views of what India's future should be.

slides.heading: Quit India begins
slides.body_md: The **resolution of 8 August 1942**; leaders arrested at once.

visual.caption: Quit India

slides.narration: The Cripps Mission of 1942 failed. In August 1942 the Congress adopted the Quit India resolution, on the eighth. Gandhi and other leaders were arrested at once. Young activists then organised strikes and sabotage across the country. The movement was suppressed by 1943 and 1944.

slides.narration: With the main leaders in jail from the first days, local activists and committees carried the movement forward. They called strikes and carried out sabotage. In some places they set up parallel governments, for example in Satara in Maharashtra and Medinipur in Bengal. The government suppressed the movement by 1943 and 1944.

slides.narration: How do we know Gandhi? From five kinds of source. Speeches and articles were made for the public. Private letters were for one reader, though some were written knowing they might be printed. The autobiography is a later look back. Police reports were made for officials. Newspapers were made for their own readers. Each kind has its own purpose and its own risks.

sections.heading: 1. Gandhi comes home: Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad
sections.body_md:
Gandhi returned to India in **January 1915** after about **two decades in South Africa**, where he had first used **satyagraha**, a method of non-violent resistance. On the advice of **Gokhale** he spent a year travelling across British India. In **February 1916**, at the opening of the **Banaras Hindu University**, he spoke to an audience that included the Indian elite and criticised them for neglecting the poor.

He then took part in three local campaigns. At **Champaran** in Bihar (1917) he took up the cause of **indigo peasants** and secured **security of tenure** and **freedom to cultivate crops of their choice**. In **Kheda** in Gujarat (1918) he asked the state to **remit revenue** after a crop failure. At **Ahmedabad** (1918) he intervened for **textile mill workers** who wanted better working conditions and a wage rise. These made him known among peasants and workers in different regions.

A reduction or waiver of the land revenue demanded from cultivators.

sections.heading: 2. The Rowlatt Act and the Non-Cooperation Movement
sections.body_md:
The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** allowed **detention without trial**. Gandhi called a countrywide **hartal** (a day of suspended work and protest) against it. On **13 April 1919** at **Jallianwala Bagh** in Amritsar, troops under **General Dyer** fired on an unarmed crowd and killed hundreds; estimates of the number vary.

The **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)** was combined with the **Khilafat movement**, which aimed to restore the Caliphate after the defeat of Ottoman Turkey, so as to bring Hindus and Muslims together. It involved the **boycott** of government schools, colleges, law courts, government jobs and foreign cloth, and the **surrender of titles**. **Constructive work** meant khadi and the charkha, Hindu–Muslim unity and ending untouchability.

In February 1922, at **Chauri Chaura**, a crowd set fire to a police station and policemen were killed. Gandhi **called off** the movement. He was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years for sedition, and was released in 1924 on grounds of health. Some leaders and followers were disappointed by the decision.

sections.heading: 3. Gandhi's appeal and the many readings of the movement
sections.body_md:
Gandhi dressed and lived simply and spoke the language of ordinary people. **Rumours of miraculous powers** spread about him, as the historian **Shahid Amin** found in a study of **Gorakhpur**. Local leaders and the Congress organisation carried his message, and **businessmen** such as **G. D. Birla** supported the Congress.

Different groups understood the movement in **their own ways**: peasants withheld taxes, tribal groups defied forest laws, and others gave swaraj a meaning of their own. So the movement was not simply what the Congress programme said it should be.

sections.heading: 4. Civil Disobedience and the march to Dandi
sections.body_md:
The all-British **Simon Commission** (1928) was boycotted. At **Lahore** in **December 1929**, with **Jawaharlal Nehru** as president, the Congress declared **purna swaraj**, complete independence, as its goal, and **26 January 1930** was celebrated as Independence Day.

Gandhi announced a march to break the **salt law**, the state's monopoly on making and selling salt, and wrote to the Viceroy, **Lord Irwin**, in advance. The **Dandi March** began on **12 March 1930** from the Sabarmati ashram and reached **Dandi** on the coast on **6 April 1930**, about 240 miles, where he made salt. Civil disobedience spread: salt was made in many places, **forest laws** were broken, **taxes** were withheld, **foreign cloth** was boycotted and **women** took part widely. Gandhi was arrested in May 1930. Foreign newspapers reported the march, which brought it world attention.

sections.heading: 5. The dialogues, separate electorates and the elections of 1937
sections.body_md:
The **First Round Table Conference** (London, November 1930) met without the Congress. The **Gandhi–Irwin Pact** (March 1931) called off civil disobedience, released prisoners and allowed salt manufacture along the coast. Gandhi attended the **Second Round Table Conference** (late 1931) as the **sole representative of the Congress**. It failed: the **Muslim League**, the **princes** and **B. R. Ambedkar**, for the depressed classes, challenged the Congress's claim to represent all. Civil disobedience resumed, then wound down.

In **1932** the British announced **separate electorates** for the depressed classes (the **Communal Award**). **Ambedkar** argued that they needed their own representatives, chosen by their own voters. **Gandhi** opposed this, fearing a lasting division of Hindu society, and fasted. The **Poona Pact** (September 1932) gave **reserved seats** in the general electorates instead.

The **Government of India Act of 1935** promised representative government. In the **1937** elections the Congress won in **8 of the 11 provinces** and formed ministries.

sections.heading: 6. Quit India and the last days
sections.body_md:
The Second World War began in **September 1939**. The Viceroy declared India at war without consulting Indians, and the **Congress ministries resigned** (October–November 1939). In **1940** the **Muslim League** at Lahore adopted a resolution demanding independent states for the areas where Muslims were in a majority. The **Cripps Mission** of 1942 failed.

The **Quit India movement** began in **August 1942** (resolution of **8 August**). **Gandhi and other leaders were arrested at once**. Young activists organised strikes and sabotage across the country, and **parallel governments** were set up in some places, such as **Satara** in Maharashtra and **Medinipur** in Bengal. The movement was suppressed by 1943–44. Gandhi was released in 1944 and held talks with **Jinnah**. **Subhas Chandra Bose** formed the **Indian National Army**.

After the war the **Cabinet Mission (1946)** proposed a loose federation, which broke down. The League called **Direct Action Day** on **16 August 1946**, followed by violence in Calcutta and then elsewhere (Noakhali, Bihar, Punjab). Gandhi walked through **Noakhali** and later worked for peace in Bihar and Calcutta. On **15 August 1947** he was in Calcutta working for communal harmony, not at the celebrations in Delhi. He was **assassinated** on **30 January 1948** in Delhi; his death was widely mourned. The Congress and the League each gave its own arguments about India's future: the Congress spoke for Indians of every community, the League for Muslims who in its view needed their own states.

sections.heading: 7. Knowing Gandhi: sources and how to read them
sections.body_md:
**Speeches** and **articles** (in journals such as **Harijan**) were meant for the public: a public voice. **Private letters** may show other feelings, but some were written with the knowledge that they might be published. His **autobiography**, *The Story of My Experiments with Truth*, written in **Gujarati** in the **1920s**, is a **retrospective** account shaped by memory and purpose.

**Government records** include secret **fortnightly reports** of the police and the Home Department. They show the officials' fears and sometimes **misread events**; some reports played down the response to the Dandi March, which other evidence contradicts. **Newspapers** in English and in Indian languages tracked Gandhi's movements and reported what he said, but they were shaped by the paper's **politics and readers**, so pro-British and nationalist papers differed.

Historians **compare** these sources. In a source question, ask: who made it, for whom and why; what it records; and what it leaves out. Part (a) is recall, part (b) an inference, part (c) two linked points.

key_terms.definition_md: An account written long after the events, shaped by memory and by the writer's purpose.
A secret official report on the state of a district, made every two weeks.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that satyagraha began in India; it was first used in South Africa.
- Saying that Non-Cooperation ended after Jallianwala Bagh; it was called off after Chauri Chaura in 1922.
- Giving a single number killed at Jallianwala Bagh; write hundreds, with estimates varying.
- Taking a side in the dispute over separate electorates or between the Congress and the League; state each side's argument.
- Describing the violence of 1946–47 in detail or blaming one community.
- Treating a police report, a newspaper or an autobiography as a neutral witness.

**How marks are awarded**
- **1 mark:** one correct fact, name or date.
- **2 marks:** two points, each with a short explanation.
- **3 marks:** three points or a reason with evidence.
- **5 marks:** an introduction, developed points on each side where asked, and a judgement for assess questions.
- **Source questions (4 marks):** (a) 1 mark for recall, (b) 1 mark for one inference, (c) 2 marks for two linked points, either of the two alternatives.

questions.stem_md: In which year did Gandhi return to India after his long stay in South Africa?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1915. He came back in January 1915. The other years belong to later or earlier events.

questions.stem_md: What did the indigo peasants of Champaran obtain through the campaign of 1917?

options.text_md: A remission of revenue after the failure of their crops
A rise in the wages paid to mill workers
The withdrawal of a law allowing detention without trial
Security of tenure and the freedom to cultivate crops of their own choice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Security of tenure and the freedom to cultivate crops of their own choice. The peasants gained security on their holdings and a say in what to grow. Remission of revenue was the issue at Kheda, and wages the issue at Ahmedabad.

questions.stem_md: Which pairing of place and group is correct for the local campaigns in which Gandhi took part in 1917 and 1918?

options.text_md: Kheda: cultivators who asked that revenue be remitted after crop failure; Ahmedabad: textile mill workers
Champaran: textile mill workers; Ahmedabad: cultivators of cotton
Kheda: indigo peasants; Champaran: cultivators who asked for remission of revenue
Ahmedabad: indigo peasants; Kheda: textile mill workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Kheda: cultivators who asked that revenue be remitted after crop failure; Ahmedabad: textile mill workers. Each pairing in the other options swaps a group between two disputes.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that the campaign at Champaran in 1917 helped to make Gandhi known beyond his own region. Which finding about an imagined set of newspapers of 1917 would most weaken this claim?

options.text_md: Papers in several provinces reported the official inquiry into the peasants' complaints
A Bihar paper praised the campaign more warmly than another paper did
Papers outside Bihar carried no report of the campaign, and almost everyone who had heard of it lived in Bihar
Papers differed on how many peasants had given statements

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Papers outside Bihar carried no report of the campaign, and almost everyone who had heard of it lived in Bihar. The claim is about how far his name travelled. Only the first finding shows his name staying inside one province; the others leave the claim standing.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated letter from a friend says that Gandhi has settled at an ashram in Gujarat after his years abroad, that he is travelling by railway in the cheapest class to see the country as an older leader advised, and that he has not yet taken up any dispute of peasants or workers. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: After the Rowlatt Act of 1919, since he has settled at an ashram
Before 1915, since he is described as travelling
After January 1915 and before the Champaran campaign of 1917, probably within his first year at home
After 1922, since he is described as a settled leader

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** After January 1915 and before the Champaran campaign of 1917, probably within his first year at home. His return from abroad sets the earliest date, and the absence of any local dispute sets the latest. The later options ignore one of these clues.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Gandhi first used the method of satyagraha at Champaran, after his return to India.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** He had first used satyagraha in South Africa, where he had spent about two decades before returning.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined records of 1917 disagree. A planter's agent writes that the tenants of an indigo district are content. A lawyer's note lists several hundred written statements of grievance taken from the same district. Give two ways in which a historian could test which record is nearer the truth.
questions.solution_md: Two tests: examine the statements, and set both records against evidence neither writer controlled.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) She could read the **statements themselves**, noting who gave them, how they were taken and whether tenants of different villages repeat the same complaints. (2) She could compare both records with **independent evidence**, such as land and rent registers, since each writer has a stake in the matter.

marking_scheme.step: Examining the statements and how they were taken

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the campaigns of Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad in 1917 and 1918 made Gandhi a national leader.
questions.solution_md: What the campaigns gave, what they could not give, and a verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Background:** he returned in 1915 after about twenty years in South Africa and spent a year travelling.
2. **What the campaigns gave him:** a hearing among peasants and workers, and proof that satyagraha could work in India.
3. **Limits:** each dispute was local, in a different region, about particular grievances, and none raised the question of self-rule.
4. **What came later:** the countrywide hartal against the Rowlatt Act in 1919 and Non-Cooperation gave him the national stage.
5. **Judgement:** the campaigns made him known and trusted in several regions, but national leadership came only with the later movements.

marking_scheme.step: The later movements as the national stage

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined officer's letter, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** He returned in 1915 and was at Champaran in 1917.

**(b)** Read the change from fear to statements as a sign of trust.

**(c) (i)** Two independent records that can confirm or correct the statements.

**OR (c) (ii)** The writer's position and a missing side, with a record that supplies it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Gandhi.**

**(b)** They came to **trust him** and believed that he would take their complaints seriously.

**(c) (i)** (1) **The planters' own records and agreements**, to test what the tenants say they were made to do. (2) **Land and rent registers** of the villages, to check the tenants' holdings and what they paid.

**OR (c) (ii)** The officer reports **what he saw and was told**, from the government's side, and he admits he has not yet seen the planters' account. A historian should read it with the **planters' own papers** or with the tenants' signed statements.

questions.passage_md:
**A sub-divisional officer's letter to his superior (imagined)**

A visitor from western India has spent some weeks in my sub-division, listening to tenants who grow indigo for the planters. Several hundred tenants have come forward to give their statements, though many were afraid of the planters' agents when he arrived. Each statement is written down and the tenant is asked to sign or put a mark to it. Lawyers from the provincial capital are helping him. The planters' agents call him an agitator and want him sent away. I think that expelling him would only draw more attention to the complaints, and an official inquiry may serve better. I have not yet looked into the planters' own account of their dealings.

children.stem_md: Name the visitor, who had come back to India from South Africa only two years earlier.
children.solution_md: He returned in 1915 and was at Champaran in 1917.

answer.model_answer_md: **Gandhi.**

children.stem_md: The officer says that many tenants were afraid at first but that hundreds have now come forward. What does this suggest about how the tenants saw the visitor?
children.solution_md: Read the change from fear to statements as a sign of trust.

answer.model_answer_md: They came to **trust him** and believed that he would take their complaints seriously.

marking_scheme.step: The tenants trusted him enough to speak

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): If the government held an inquiry, name two kinds of evidence it would need besides the tenants' statements, and say what each would test.
children.solution_md: Two independent records that can confirm or correct the statements.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **The planters' own records and agreements**, to test what the tenants say they were made to do. (2) **Land and rent registers** of the villages, to check the tenants' holdings and what they paid.

marking_scheme.step: Planters' records and what they test
Land and rent registers and what they test

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain why a historian should not treat this letter alone as a full account of the dispute, and name one other record she should read with it.
alternatives.solution_md: The writer's position and a missing side, with a record that supplies it.

answer.model_answer_md: The officer reports **what he saw and was told**, from the government's side, and he admits he has not yet seen the planters' account. A historian should read it with the **planters' own papers** or with the tenants' signed statements.

marking_scheme.step: The letter gives one official's partial view
A named record to set beside it

questions.stem_md: What did the Rowlatt Act of 1919 allow the government to do?

options.text_md: Detain people without trial
Raise the tax on salt
Ban the import of foreign cloth
Dismiss the ministers of the provinces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Detain people without trial. The Act allowed detention without trial. Gandhi called a countrywide hartal against it.

questions.stem_md: Estimates of the number killed at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919 differ. Imagine that an official inquiry and an inquiry by a non-official committee each gave a different figure. Which question would best help a historian decide which figure is more reliable?

options.text_md: Which body's report was printed first?
Which body had the more senior members?
Which figure is easier to remember?
How did each body collect its figures: from hospital, cremation and family records, or only from the accounts of those who were present?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** How did each body collect its figures: from hospital, cremation and family records, or only from the accounts of those who were present? Reliability depends on method and records. Priority of printing, rank of members and ease of memory say nothing about how a number was reached.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that joining the Khilafat cause to the Non-Cooperation Movement drew Hindus and Muslims into joint action. Which finding about imagined towns would most weaken this claim?

options.text_md: Records showing that Khilafat meetings in many towns were addressed by speakers of the Congress
Records showing that in most towns the Khilafat committee and the Congress committee held separate meetings and never acted together
Records showing that Muslim volunteers joined the picketing of cloth shops in towns with a Khilafat committee
Records showing that the Khilafat cause was explained in Hindi and Urdu newspapers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Records showing that in most towns the Khilafat committee and the Congress committee held separate meetings and never acted together. The claim concerns joint action. Only separate meetings with no joint action cut against it; the other findings show or allow cooperation.

questions.stem_md: Which of these was NOT part of the programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22?

options.text_md: Boycott of a commission with no Indian member
Boycott of foreign cloth
Surrender of titles given by the government
Boycott of law courts, schools and colleges run by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Boycott of a commission with no Indian member. The boycott of an all-British commission belongs to 1928, not to 1920–22. The other three were forms of non-cooperation.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that peasants, workers and tribal groups understood swaraj in their own ways during the Non-Cooperation Movement, rather than simply following the Congress's programme. Which finding about an imagined hill district would most strengthen this claim?

options.text_md: Records showing that a Congress committee asked villagers to boycott foreign cloth and that they did so
Records showing that villagers defied forest rules and refused grazing fees, saying that swaraj meant freedom from such rules, though no Congress committee had asked them to
Records showing that lawyers of the district gave up their practice
Records showing that the collector banned a public meeting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Records showing that villagers defied forest rules and refused grazing fees, saying that swaraj meant freedom from such rules, though no Congress committee had asked them to. The claim is that local groups gave the movement their own meaning. Action they took without being asked, justified in their own terms, shows that; the other findings show the programme being followed or the state responding.

questions.stem_md: A historian wants to study how rumours about Gandhi's miraculous powers spread among villagers of one district in 1921–22. Which source would be most useful?

options.text_md: Gandhi's own account of his early life
A speech of the Viceroy to the legislature
Reports of officials about what villagers were saying, read together with recollections gathered later from villagers
A table of the revenue collected in the district

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Reports of officials about what villagers were saying, read together with recollections gathered later from villagers. Rumours are about what ordinary people believed and passed on. Officials noted what they heard, and villagers' memories add the other side; the other sources do not touch popular belief.

questions.stem_md: What happened at Chauri Chaura in February 1922?

options.text_md: Troops fired on an unarmed gathering
Gandhi began a march to the sea
Mill workers went on strike
A crowd set fire to a police station and policemen were killed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A crowd set fire to a police station and policemen were killed. This violence led Gandhi to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement. The firing on a gathering was at Jallianwala Bagh in 1919.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated handbill urges townspeople to turn out with black flags against a visiting commission that has no Indian member. It adds that the Congress will meet at Lahore the next year and decide its goal. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: In 1929, after the Lahore session
In 1930, during the salt campaign
In 1920, at the start of Non-Cooperation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** In 1928. The commission with no Indian member is the one boycotted in 1928, and the Lahore session was held in December 1929, which was still the next year.

questions.stem_md: Which law did Gandhi choose to break at the end of the march of 1930?

options.text_md: A ban on spinning cotton at home
A rule that forest produce be sold only to the government
The law giving the state a monopoly on making and selling salt
A rule that peasants must grow indigo for planters

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The law giving the state a monopoly on making and selling salt. He made salt on the coast, in defiance of the state's monopoly. The other rules belong to other grievances.

questions.stem_md: An imagined letter from a volunteer says: we left the ashram some days ago; each evening villagers feed us and the crowds grow; the sea is still some days away; the letter to the Viceroy was sent before we set out. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: After 6 April 1930, once salt had been made
Between 12 March and 6 April 1930
In 1931, after the pact with the Viceroy
In January 1930, before the march was announced

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Between 12 March and 6 April 1930. The march began on 12 March and ended at the sea on 6 April. A letter written on the road, with the sea still ahead, falls between the two dates.

questions.stem_md: An imagined police table for one coastal district in 1930 gives, for four successive fortnights, the number of salt-making incidents and of arrests: 12 incidents and 30 arrests; 40 and 95; 25 and 120; 10 and 140. Which reading is best supported?

options.text_md: Arrests per incident rose from 2.5 to 14, so either more people were arrested for each act or arrests were made for other acts; the table cannot tell which
Incidents and arrests rose together at the same rate in every fortnight
The campaign was dying out, since incidents fell to 10
The police made fewer arrests as the campaign went on

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Arrests per incident rose from 2.5 to 14, so either more people were arrested for each act or arrests were made for other acts; the table cannot tell which. Thirty arrests over 12 incidents is 2.5 each; 140 over 10 is 14. A fall in incidents does not show a campaign dying, because the arrests themselves may have discouraged action; and the table does not say what the arrests were for.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated letter says that prisoners are being released, that people on the coast may again make salt, that civil disobedience has been stopped, and that the writer's friend is getting ready for a voyage to London. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: Before the First Round Table Conference of November 1930
After March 1931 and before the Second Round Table Conference of late 1931
After the Poona Pact of September 1932
In 1942, during the Quit India movement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** After March 1931 and before the Second Round Table Conference of late 1931. Prisoners freed and civil disobedience stopped belong to the agreement of March 1931, and the journey to London points to the conference that followed it.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that the Second Round Table Conference of 1931 failed mainly because of disputes over who represented whom. Which finding about an imagined record of the conference would most weaken this?

options.text_md: Records showing that the League, the princes and Ambedkar each disputed the Congress's claim to speak for all
Records showing that Gandhi attended as the Congress's only representative
Records showing that the conference met in London in the autumn
Records showing that the delegates had settled the question of representation within the first days, and that talks broke down over some other matter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Records showing that the delegates had settled the question of representation within the first days, and that talks broke down over some other matter. The explanation puts representation first. Finding that it was settled and that something else ended the talks removes its force; the other findings are facts that fit it.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: In 1932 the Poona Pact accepted Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates for the depressed classes and ended Gandhi's fast. Which comment finds the flaw?

options.text_md: The Pact gave reserved seats within the general electorates in place of separate electorates, so the original demand was modified, not accepted as it stood
The fast was undertaken by Ambedkar, not by Gandhi
The Pact was signed in 1930, not in 1932
The statement is correct as it stands

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Pact gave reserved seats within the general electorates in place of separate electorates, so the original demand was modified, not accepted as it stood. The statement is right that the Pact ended the fast but wrong about what it gave. Reserved seats in the general electorates were the compromise.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gandhi was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years for sedition.

**Reason (R):** Gandhi had called off the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are accurate, but the second does not explain the first: the sentence was a decision of the government, taken on a charge of sedition, whereas the second states a decision of Gandhi's own.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At the Second Round Table Conference Gandhi's claim to speak for all Indians was challenged.

**Reason (R):** The Muslim League, the princes and Ambedkar each claimed to speak for their own groups.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Each of these claims set a limit on what the Congress could say it represented, which is how the challenge arose.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Non-Cooperation Movement was called off after the firing at Jallianwala Bagh.

**Reason (R):** Gandhi was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The firing of 1919 came before the movement began; it was called off in 1922 after Chauri Chaura. The statement about the sentence is accurate.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Poona Pact of 1932 gave the depressed classes reserved seats in the general electorates.

**Reason (R):** Gandhi's fast against separate electorates led to talks in which Ambedkar took part.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The talks that followed the fast produced the pact, so the second statement accounts for how the first came about.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the elections of 1937 the Congress won in all the provinces of British India and formed ministries in every one.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It won in eight of the eleven provinces and formed ministries there.

questions.stem_md: The Lahore session of the Congress in December ___ declared purna swaraj as its goal; its president was ___.
questions.solution_md: The session was held in 1929 under Jawaharlal Nehru, and 26 January 1930 was then celebrated as Independence Day.

questions.stem_md: Match each name with the correct description.

options.text_md: Jawaharlal Nehru
General Dyer
Lord Irwin
B. R. Ambedkar

match_right.text_md: Officer whose troops fired on the crowd at Jallianwala Bagh
Leader who argued for separate electorates for the depressed classes
President of the Congress session at Lahore in 1929
Viceroy to whom Gandhi wrote before the march of 1930

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each name is linked with one episode of the years 1919 to 1932.

questions.stem_md: Match each measure with what it provided.

options.text_md: Rowlatt Act
Communal Award
Poona Pact
Gandhi–Irwin Pact

match_right.text_md: Called off civil disobedience and released prisoners
Gave reserved seats in the general electorates
Announced separate electorates for the depressed classes

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each measure belongs to a different stage of the years 1919 to 1932.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of the years 1929 to 1937 in chronological order, earliest first.

options.text_md: The Congress wins eight of eleven provinces
The Congress at Lahore declares purna swaraj
The Poona Pact
The Gandhi–Irwin Pact
Gandhi reaches Dandi and makes salt

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (d) → (c) → (a). They fall in December 1929, April 1930, March 1931, September 1932 and 1937.

questions.stem_md: Describe in two points what happened at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919.
questions.solution_md: The firing and its setting, with the uncertainty of the figures.

answer.model_answer_md: A crowd had gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar. **Troops under General Dyer fired on the unarmed crowd** and killed hundreds. Estimates of the number killed **vary** between sources. It happened while the country was protesting against the Rowlatt Act.

marking_scheme.step: Firing by troops under Dyer on an unarmed crowd

questions.stem_md: State two forms taken by the Non-Cooperation Movement.
questions.solution_md: Two of the forms of withdrawal from government institutions and goods.

answer.model_answer_md: People were asked to **boycott** government schools, colleges, law courts and jobs, and to boycott **foreign cloth**, taking up khadi and the charkha instead. They were also asked to **surrender the titles** the government had given them.

questions.stem_md: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922, and what happened to him soon afterwards?
questions.solution_md: The violence, his decision and its sequel.

answer.model_answer_md: At Chauri Chaura a crowd set fire to a police station and policemen were killed. The movement was meant to be non-violent, so Gandhi **called it off**. He was **arrested in March 1922** and sentenced to six years for sedition, and was released in 1924 because of ill health.

marking_scheme.step: The violence at Chauri Chaura as the reason

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why a march to make salt could draw support from people of many different groups.
questions.solution_md: The reach of the grievance and the simplicity of the act.

answer.model_answer_md: Salt was used in **every household**, so the state's monopoly on making and selling it touched rich and poor alike. Making salt at the coast was also a **simple, open and non-violent act** that anyone could understand and copy.

questions.stem_md: State the main argument made by each side in the dispute of 1932 over separate electorates for the depressed classes.
questions.solution_md: Each side's argument in its own terms, then the compromise.

answer.model_answer_md: **Ambedkar** argued that separate electorates would give the depressed classes their own representatives, chosen by their own voters. **Gandhi** opposed them, fearing a lasting division of Hindu society, and fasted. The **Poona Pact** settled the matter with reserved seats in the general electorates.

questions.stem_md: An imagined fortnightly police report says that the Dandi March passed with little public interest, while a newspaper of the same days describes large crowds at every halt. Give two ways of reconciling the accounts without calling either writer a liar.
questions.solution_md: Two ways in which honest accounts can differ: vantage and purpose, or place and time.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The officer may have relied on **informers who saw little**, or on an official's wish to see weak support, while the paper wrote for sympathetic readers. (2) The two may describe **different places or days**, so each is true of what its writer saw.

marking_scheme.step: A difference of vantage or purpose
A difference of place or day

questions.stem_md: A historian finds a village register of an imagined district, dated 1930, that lists sixty names under the heading volunteers for the salt campaign. State one thing she can conclude from it and one thing she cannot.
questions.solution_md: What a list of names shows and what it leaves open.

answer.model_answer_md: She can conclude that the campaign had **organised volunteers** in that village, who enrolled by name. She cannot conclude **how many actually took part** or why each joined, since enrolling is not the same as acting and the register records no motives.

marking_scheme.step: A sound conclusion from the register
A limit on what it shows

questions.stem_md: An imagined district reports pupils in government schools as 500 in 1920, 320 in 1921 and 410 in 1922, and shops stocking foreign cloth as 80, 45 and 70. Work out the percentage fall in each series from 1920 to 1921, and explain the partial recovery in 1922 using what you know of how the movement ended.
questions.solution_md: Two percentages, a link to the end of the movement and a caution about what figures can prove.

answer.model_answer_md: Pupils fell by 180 of 500, **36 per cent**; shops by 35 of 80, about **44 per cent**. The recovery in 1922 fits the movement being **called off after Chauri Chaura in February 1922**, which ended the call to boycott. The figures alone cannot prove this, since other causes may also have been at work.

marking_scheme.step: Recovery linked to the calling off of the movement
Caution that the figures alone do not prove the cause

questions.stem_md: Describe three ways in which civil disobedience spread across the country after the march to Dandi.
questions.solution_md: Salt-making elsewhere, defiance of forest laws and taxes, and the boycott with women's participation.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) People in many places **made salt** or broke other laws in the same open way. (2) **Forest laws were defied** and **taxes were withheld** in some areas. (3) **Foreign cloth was boycotted**, and **women took part** widely. Arrests followed, among them Gandhi's own in May 1930.

questions.stem_md: Explain three reasons why the Second Round Table Conference of 1931 failed to produce an agreement.
questions.solution_md: The Congress claim and the three challenges to it.

answer.model_answer_md: Gandhi attended as the **sole representative of the Congress** and spoke for all Indians. This was challenged by the **Muslim League**, which spoke for Muslims, by the **princes**, and by **B. R. Ambedkar**, who spoke for the depressed classes. The disputes over representation were not settled, so the conference ended without agreement.

marking_scheme.step: Challenges from the League, the princes and Ambedkar

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Poona Pact of 1932 came about and what it provided.
questions.solution_md: The award, the fast and the compromise.

answer.model_answer_md: In 1932 the British announced **separate electorates** for the depressed classes, which Ambedkar had argued for so that they would have their own representatives. Gandhi opposed them and **fasted**. After talks with Ambedkar, the **Poona Pact** of September 1932 gave the depressed classes **reserved seats** within the general electorates instead.

questions.stem_md: A historian wants to find out how ordinary people along the coast responded to the march of 1930. Name three kinds of source she could use and state one limit of each.
questions.solution_md: Three kinds of source, each paired with the limit that comes from who made it.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Fortnightly police reports**, which record meetings and arrests but reflect the officials' fears. (2) **Newspapers in Indian languages**, which report local events but reflect their politics and their readers. (3) **Letters or diaries of volunteers**, which give a view from inside but are few and may be written for a purpose.

marking_scheme.step: Letters or diaries with a limit

questions.stem_md: An imagined fortnightly report from a town says that cloth shops were picketed as follows: 12 in the first fortnight, 30 in the second and 20 in the third. Of these, 3, 12 and 10 shops agreed to stop selling foreign cloth. Work out the share that agreed in each fortnight, state one inference and state one limit of the report.
questions.solution_md: Three divisions, a reading of the trend and a limit.

answer.model_answer_md: The shares were **25, 40 and 50 per cent**. The share of picketed shops that agreed rose, so picketing may have grown more effective, or shopkeepers felt more public pressure. But this is an official's tally and does not show **why** shops agreed or whether they went back to foreign cloth later.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–22: its background, its forms, the groups that joined it and how it ended.
questions.solution_md: Causes, forms, participants and the end of the movement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Background:** the Rowlatt Act of 1919 and the firing at Jallianwala Bagh angered many Indians; the Khilafat cause was joined to the movement to bring Hindus and Muslims together.
2. **Forms:** boycott of schools, colleges, courts, government jobs and foreign cloth, and surrender of titles; khadi and the charkha were promoted.
3. **Groups:** peasants, workers and tribal people took part, each understanding swaraj in their own way.
4. **End:** after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, Gandhi called it off.
5. **Sequel:** he was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years.

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the Gandhi–Irwin Pact and the Round Table Conferences achieved the aims with which the Congress had begun civil disobedience.
questions.solution_md: The aims, the gains, the failure of the conference and a measured verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Aims:** the Congress declared purna swaraj at Lahore in 1929, and the salt march of 1930 began civil disobedience.
2. **Gains of the Pact (1931):** civil disobedience was called off, prisoners were released and salt-making along the coast was allowed.
3. **The conferences:** the Second Round Table Conference of 1931 ended without agreement, as the League, the princes and Ambedkar challenged the Congress's claim to speak for all.
4. **After:** civil disobedience resumed and then wound down; the Act of 1935 promised representative government, and the Congress won eight of eleven provinces in 1937.
5. **Judgement:** complete independence was not reached, but the Congress gained a hearing and a place in government.

questions.stem_md: Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement after Chauri Chaura. Weigh the arguments for and against that decision and give a judgement.
questions.solution_md: The event, a case on each side, a caution about hindsight and a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The event:** a crowd burnt a police station and policemen were killed in February 1922.
2. **For the decision:** the movement was to be non-violent, and violence might bring harsher repression and lose the movement's moral ground.
3. **Against it:** many leaders and followers were disappointed, the movement was widespread at the time, and Gandhi was arrested soon afterwards.
4. **Caution:** these judgements are made with hindsight; the participants had less information than we do.
5. **Judgement:** the decision followed from a principle; its cost was a loss of momentum, so neither wholly right nor wholly wrong.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined police officer's fortnightly report, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** He wrote to the Viceroy in advance of the march.

**(b)** Set the opening verdict against the facts he reports.

**(c) (i)** Two products and a reading of them against his verdict.

**OR (c) (ii)** The writer's position and the need for other sources.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined newspaper report, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** He negotiated the agreement that came to be called the Poona Pact.

**(b)** Read the closing hope as a sign of the paper's sympathies.

**(c) (i)** Two emphases that follow from a different readership.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two sources that reach the reasons behind a view.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **B. R. Ambedkar.**

**(b)** The paper is **sympathetic to the nationalist leaders**, and it reads the agreement as a success for national unity.

**(c) (i)** (1) **The argument for their own representatives**, since the paper would care most for that demand. (2) **What the agreement gave and did not give**, since its readers would judge it by what it meant for their own representation.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) **His own speeches and writings** of the time, which would give his reasons in his own words. (2) **Records of the talks** kept by others present, which would show how each side argued and what was conceded.

**A nationalist daily's report from Poona, September 1932 (imagined)**

Crowds waited all day outside the jail where the Mahatma, weak after several days without food, lay on his cot. Inside the city, leaders of the caste Hindus and leaders of the depressed classes sat in long talks. The depressed classes' leaders argued that their people needed seats chosen by their own voters, since the experience of centuries had taught them not to trust others to speak for them. The Mahatma's friends replied that the nation must stay one. After days of anxiety an agreement was announced and the crowds cheered. Our paper hopes that this day will be remembered as the beginning of a new fellowship among all our people.

children.solution_md: He negotiated the agreement that came to be called the Poona Pact.

answer.model_answer_md: **B. R. Ambedkar.**

children.solution_md: Read the closing hope as a sign of the paper's sympathies.

answer.model_answer_md: The paper is **sympathetic to the nationalist leaders**, and it reads the agreement as a success for national unity.

children.solution_md: Two emphases that follow from a different readership.

Stress on what the agreement gave or withheld

alternatives.solution_md: Two sources that reach the reasons behind a view.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **His own speeches and writings** of the time, which would give his reasons in his own words. (2) **Records of the talks** kept by others present, which would show how each side argued and what was conceded.

questions.stem_md: An imagined, undated letter says that the movement of two years ago is now being put down for good, that its main leader has lately been released on grounds of health and has begun talks with Jinnah, and that the war has not yet ended. Which dating is soundest?

options.text_md: In 1942, just after the resolution of August
In 1946, during the Cabinet Mission
In 1944, after his release and before the end of the war
In 1948, after his death

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** In 1944, after his release and before the end of the war. The movement began in August 1942; his release and the talks with Jinnah came in 1944, while the war was still on.

questions.stem_md: What did the Muslim League demand in its resolution at Lahore in 1940?

options.text_md: Separate electorates for the depressed classes
The immediate departure of the British from India
Independent states for the areas where Muslims were in a majority
A rule that the Congress ministries resign

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Independent states for the areas where Muslims were in a majority. The resolution asked for independent states in the Muslim-majority areas. The other options describe other demands or events.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: In the mid-1940s the Congress and the League disagreed only because each party wanted to hold office. Which comment finds the main flaw?

options.text_md: It leaves out the arguments each side gave: the Congress said that it spoke for Indians of every community, while the League said that it represented Muslims and that they needed their own states
It wrongly says that the Congress took part in the talks
It wrongly says that the League existed in the 1940s
It is correct, since all parties seek office

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It leaves out the arguments each side gave: the Congress said that it spoke for Indians of every community, while the League said that it represented Muslims and that they needed their own states. A fair account sets out each side's argument. Reducing a political dispute to a wish for office leaves out what each party said it stood for.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: Gandhi was in Calcutta on 15 August 1947 and not at the celebrations in Delhi, so he must have opposed independence. Which comment finds the flaw?

options.text_md: It is correct, since a leader who stays away from a celebration opposes its purpose
It wrongly places him in Calcutta, since he was in Delhi that day
It wrongly gives 15 August 1947 as the date of the transfer of power
It infers his view from where he was, although he was working in Calcutta for communal harmony; his view of independence must be judged from what he said and did, which this fact does not show

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It infers his view from where he was, although he was working in Calcutta for communal harmony; his view of independence must be judged from what he said and did, which this fact does not show. Absence from an event is weak evidence of opposition to it. A historian needs his own statements and actions, and here the record shows him engaged in work for peace elsewhere.

questions.stem_md: When and where was Gandhi assassinated?

options.text_md: 15 August 1947, in Calcutta
30 January 1948, in Delhi
26 January 1950, in Delhi
2 October 1948, in Ahmedabad

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 30 January 1948, in Delhi. He was shot on 30 January 1948 at Delhi. His death was widely mourned.

questions.stem_md: Some historians say that Gandhi's presence in Calcutta in August 1947 helped to keep the city calm in those weeks. Which finding about an imagined set of records would most weaken that claim?

options.text_md: Records showing that the city was already calm before he arrived, and that districts he never visited were as calm as the city
Records showing that large crowds of Hindus and Muslims attended his prayer meetings
Records showing that local peace committees credited his presence
Records showing that police reports noted fewer incidents in the city during his stay

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Records showing that the city was already calm before he arrived, and that districts he never visited were as calm as the city. To weaken a claim of influence, look for the same outcome without the supposed cause. Calm that came earlier and elsewhere without him makes his presence less likely to be the reason.

questions.stem_md: Historians say that Quit India grew into a widespread movement chiefly through the actions of local activists after the main leaders were in jail. Which finding about an imagined district would most weaken this claim for that district?

options.text_md: Records showing that a student group called the first strike
Records showing that strikes and sabotage began there only after a written plan from the jailed leaders was circulated by their agents, and that no local group acted before it
Records showing that local men set up a parallel government
Records showing that the police arrested local organisers within days

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Records showing that strikes and sabotage began there only after a written plan from the jailed leaders was circulated by their agents, and that no local group acted before it. The claim gives the initiative to local people. Action that waited for a plan from the leaders removes that, while the other findings show local initiative or the state's response.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Congress ministries resigned in October and November 1939.

**Reason (R):** In the elections of 1937 the Congress had won in eight of the eleven provinces.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are accurate, but the second explains why the Congress held ministries, not why they resigned. The resignations followed the declaration of war on India's behalf without consulting Indians.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Cabinet Mission's proposal of 1946 for a loose federation broke down.

**Reason (R):** Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946 was followed by violence in Calcutta and elsewhere.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are accurate, but the second does not account for the first. The proposal had already failed to hold when Direct Action Day was called, so the violence followed the breakdown rather than causing it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Quit India movement spread widely in 1942 even though the main leaders of the Congress were in jail from the first days.

**Reason (R):** The movement was directed throughout by detailed daily instructions from those leaders.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The movement did spread, but with the leaders arrested at once it could not have been directed by them day by day; local activists organised much of it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? On 15 August 1947 Gandhi took part in the celebrations at Delhi.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** He was in Calcutta, working for harmony between communities.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of the years 1939 to 1946 in chronological order, earliest first.

options.text_md: The League's resolution at Lahore
Gandhi's work for peace in Noakhali
The Cabinet Mission
The Quit India resolution
The Congress ministries resign

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). They fall in October and November 1939, 1940, August 1942, the spring of 1946 and the winter of 1946.

questions.stem_md: An imagined diary entry says: the leaders of the Congress were taken away this morning; the Viceroy's talks with the visiting mission failed earlier this year; the city is on strike. In which month and year was it most probably written, and which two clues support this?
questions.solution_md: A date reasoned from two clues.

answer.model_answer_md: Probably **August 1942**. The arrest of the Congress leaders points to the start of the Quit India movement, and the failed talks with the visiting mission point to the Cripps Mission of earlier that year.

questions.stem_md: In many districts strikes and sabotage began within days of August 1942, although the main leaders of the Congress were arrested at once. Suggest two explanations that do not depend on messages from the leaders in jail.
questions.solution_md: Local initiative and the arrests as a trigger.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Young activists and local committees** acted on their own, so the movement did not need orders from jail. (2) The **arrests themselves may have angered people**, and the failed talks of that spring may have left them ready to act, so the arrests worked as a spark.

marking_scheme.step: Local activists acted on their own
The arrests or earlier anger as a trigger

questions.stem_md: Assess how far the course of the Quit India movement of 1942 depended on the main leaders and how far on local activists.
questions.solution_md: The part of the leaders, the part of local activists and a measured verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **The start:** the resolution of 8 August 1942 began the movement, and Gandhi and other leaders were arrested at once.
2. **The leaders:** their call and their arrest gave the movement its occasion, and the arrests may themselves have angered people.
3. **Local activists:** young activists organised strikes and sabotage, and parallel governments appeared in places such as Satara and Medinipur, without orders from jail.
4. **The end:** the government suppressed the movement by 1943–44.
5. **Judgement:** the leaders supplied the call, but most of the course of the movement was shaped locally, so it depended chiefly on local activists.

questions.stem_md: Read the source, an imagined letter between two volunteers, and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real, though the evidence and events in the background are.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Both are named among the places of parallel governments.

**(b)** Link the arrest of the leaders to decisions made on the spot.

**(c) (i)** A date reasoned from two clues.

**OR (c) (ii)** The narrowness of a single letter and the mixed picture inside it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Satara** in Maharashtra, or **Medinipur** in Bengal.

**(b)** It ran by **local initiative**, without direction from a central leadership.

**(c) (i)** **August 1942.** The leaders were taken away the day after a great meeting, which fits the arrests that followed the resolution, and the strikes, sabotage and local councils are features of that movement.

**OR (c) (ii)** (1) It is **one writer in one town**, so it cannot show what happened across the country. (2) It mentions **strikes and a council** as well as one act of sabotage, so it shows a mixed picture; a historian needs **other records**, from police files and newspapers, to judge the movement as a whole.
